general_notes.general_notes:
This study is an extension of previous work by the same research group, applying a similar normative modeling approach to investigate white matter volume heterogeneity in the same cohort of participants with psychiatric disorders.

- association_analysis: "Permutation testing was used to assess differences in the proportions of cases and controls showing extreme deviations in each voxel."
- key_findings_brief: "The prevalence of WMV deviations was lower than previously observed in gray matter, and the specific location of these deviations was highly heterogeneous when considering voxelwise spatial resolution."
- key_findings_detailed: "The specific locations of WMV deviations were highly heterogeneous across participants, affecting the same voxel in fewer than 8% of individuals with the same diagnosis. For autism and schizophrenia, negative deviations (i.e., areas where volume is lower than normative expectations) aggregated into common tracts, regions, and large-scale networks in up to 69% of individuals."
- key_limitations: "The study's limitations include the use of VBM for WMV quantification, which may not be optimal for white matter's fibrous structure; the inherent limitations of diffusion MRI tractography; the reliance on DSM-based diagnostic categories; and the potential confounding effect of total deviation burden on overlap differences."
- application_notes: "Fewer than 36% of individuals in any group showed at least 1 extreme negative WMV deviation compared to 76% for GMV deviations in our previous study. Positive WMV deviations were more common, with over 61% of people showing at least 1 extreme deviation. The authors note that it is unclear if this is a true biological phenomenon or a limitation of the normative models."
